h1: Hosting a whisky tasting evening at home for a group of friends
title: Host a Whisky Tasting at Home | Craft Beer School
desc: How to host a whisky tasting at home: choosing four or five bottles, pour sizes, running order, food, water and keeping the evening relaxed and responsible.
teaser: Four bottles, small pours, plenty of water and a running order. That is most of a good whisky evening.
standfirst: A whisky tasting at home is one of the easiest ways to learn with friends. A little planning keeps it focused on flavour, makes everyone comfortable and gets every guest home safely.
sections: Decide what the evening is about

A tasting works best with a theme. Without one, five random bottles turn into a blur. Pick one question and let the bottles answer it. Good starter themes include:

  • Cask types: an ex-bourbon matured malt against a sherry matured one.
  • Countries: an Indian single malt, a Scotch, a bourbon and a Japanese whisky.
  • Peat: from unpeated to heavily smoky.
  • Age: the same distillery at two or three ages, where you can find them.

Four or five whiskies is plenty. More than that and palates tire, conversation drifts and pours add up faster than anyone notices.
Pour sizes and the running order

Use small measured pours of about 15 ml per whisky. Five of those come to 75 ml in total over a couple of hours, which is enough to taste properly. A jigger or a small measuring cup keeps pours honest. Pouring yourself rather than leaving bottles on the table helps.

Run from light to heavy: lower strength before higher, unpeated before peated, ex-bourbon before sherry. Peat and cask strength whiskies swamp the palate, so save them for last. Write the order on a card at each seat.

You do not need rare bottles. A tasting teaches more when the whiskies are easy to find again, because guests can buy the one they liked. Mix one or two everyday bottles with one special one.

To share the cost, ask each guest to bring one bottle that fits the theme and keep a list so you do not end up with three of the same. Miniatures and sample sets are another good route for themes such as peat or cask types. Opened bottles keep well for months if stored upright and away from heat, so nothing is wasted after the evening.

Tulip shaped nosing glasses concentrate aroma best, though small wine glasses work well. One glass per whisky per guest is ideal. If you are short, rinse with water between pours. Our guide to glassware explains why the shape of the bowl changes what you smell.

Put out still water in jugs, a small dropper or teaspoon for adding water to the whisky and a separate glass of water for drinking. Spit cups or a spittoon should be on the table, used without fuss. Plain crackers or bread reset the palate between whiskies.
Food that helps rather than hides

Serve proper food before or alongside the tasting, not only snacks. Whisky on an empty stomach is a poor idea and a full table keeps the pace gentle. Grilled paneer tikka, seekh kebabs, roasted nuts, a cheese plate and dark chocolate all work.

Keep the fiercest chilli for later. Heavy spice exaggerates the burn of alcohol and blunts your sense of smell for a while. A plate of mithai after the last pour makes a fine finish.

For each whisky, give guests a minute in silence to look, nose and sip. Then ask simple questions. What do you smell first? Does it change with a few drops of water? Is it sweet, dry, spicy or smoky? Reveal the label afterwards if you are tasting blind.

Encourage people to write a word or two for each whisky. There are no wrong answers at this level. Our guide to whisky tasting for beginners gives a simple order to follow.

Tell guests the plan when you invite them, so nobody feels pressured. Make it clear that sipping and spitting is normal and that non-drinkers are welcome. Have good soft drinks on hand, such as fresh lime soda or a hop water, so anyone can join in on aroma.

Sort transport before the first pour. Arrange cabs, offer a sofa or name a sober driver. Nobody drives after a tasting, however small the pours felt. Keep whisky away from anyone under the legal drinking age in your state, which varies across India.

Hosting is a fast way to discover how much your vocabulary limits you. You smell something familiar in the glass and cannot name it. That gap is normal and it closes with structured practice: reference aromas, side-by-side comparisons and a consistent way of describing what you find.

That practice works better with a trained guide than alone, which is what sensory training is for.
faqs: How many whiskies should a home tasting have?
Four or five is enough. More than that tires the palate and adds up to more alcohol than a relaxed evening needs.
How much whisky should I pour per person?
About 15 ml per whisky is plenty to taste properly. Measure it rather than pouring by eye.
Should I add water to whisky at a tasting?
Offer it. A few drops often open up aroma, especially at higher strength. Let guests taste it neat first, then with water. Compare the two.
